sections.html:
Alabama's northwest corner belongs to Lauderdale County. Florence is the seat and the lone city, home to part of the county's 97,135 people (2025 estimate). Of 44,585 housing units, 66.7 percent of the occupied ones are owner-occupied. About half the population is rural, which means a typical seller may hold acreage rather than a city lot.

Water bounds the county on two sides, the Tennessee River to the south and west, with the Elk River and Pickwick Lake adding shoreline. Before listing a low-lying parcel, check its flood exposure. Storm or flood damage is difficult to conceal, and an as-is sale means you can leave repairs undone.

Location also sets the school district: Florence City Schools inside the city, the Lauderdale County School District outside it. Older downtown houses may sit in a historic district with rules on exterior changes, so call the city before planning any work.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
One office, the Lauderdale County Revenue Commissioner, both sets values and takes payment. October 1 is the due date. After December 31 the account is delinquent, with advertising in April and a sale in May for parcels still unpaid.

Way to payDetails
In personCash, check, money order or credit card at the Revenue Commissioner's office
By mailSend payment to the office
Onlinealproptax.com
Credit card, in person or online2.50 percent service fee

With a mortgage escrow, confirm what the lender has already sent so you do not pay twice.

sections.h2: Property classes and the homestead exemption
sections.html:
State law sorts property into three classes. Class I, utilities, is at 30 percent. Class II, other property, is at 20 percent. Class III, which holds farmland, timber and owner-occupied single-family homes, is at 10 percent. Multiply appraised value by the percentage to reach assessed value.

A homestead exemption is for a single-family home that you owned and lived in on the first day of the tax year. Four versions are on offer.

  • H1, the regular exemption: $4,000 of assessed value for state tax and $3,000 for county tax.
  • H2: owners over 65 with adjusted gross income of $12,000 or less.
  • H3: owners who are totally disabled, or over 65 with taxable income under $12,000.
  • H4: owners over 65, whatever their income.

File before December 31. Applying for an over 65 exemption means bringing a driver's license or birth certificate plus your latest federal return. The number for questions is (256) 760-5785.

sections.h2: Taxes when you buy or sell
sections.html:
After buying, an owner has four tasks: put the deed on record in probate court, have the property assessed in their own name at the Revenue Commissioner's office, claim exemptions or current use status, and wrap it all up by December 31 when the purchase predates October 1.

That year's notice will not carry the new owner's name, since the state holds the name and exemptions from the prior October 1. Buyers should therefore verify payment themselves. Owners who add or remove improvements must report that by December 31 as well.

Sellers should make sure the tax line appears on the settlement statement and hold on to the paid receipt. When tax is still owed, the closer requests a payoff from the Revenue Commissioner and takes it from your proceeds. Do this early in the sale. A late payoff request can push the closing date back by days.

A manufactured home that is not rented or leased has to be assessed at the Revenue Commissioner's office. The county asks for a bill of sale, a title 20 years old or newer and proof that sales tax was paid.

Gather those papers before you list. A gap in the title or the assessment record is the most common reason a mobile home sale stalls, and sorting it out takes longer than most sellers expect.

sections.h2: Delinquent tax and the May sale
sections.html:
The schedule is firm. After December 31 the account is delinquent, and in April the parcel is advertised. The sale follows in May. Costs rise at each step, so an early payoff is the cheapest one.

If you cannot pay and the house is the problem, a sale before May can clear the balance from the proceeds. Call the Revenue Commissioner for a current payoff, then give the figure to whoever is handling your closing.

Do not wait for a notice to start this. A bill that never reached you is still your debt, and the calendar does not pause for the mail. If you have moved away, update your mailing address with the office so later notices find you. Heirs who inherit a house should look the parcel up before the next October 1 comes around, because tax keeps accruing while title is being sorted out.

sections.h2: How a sale of rural land differs
sections.html:
Acreage brings questions a city lot does not. Does the parcel carry current use status, and would that change when ownership does? Are there outbuildings that were never reported, or ones that were torn down but still show on the record? Does the boundary match what the neighbors believe?

Bring answers to the Revenue Commissioner's office before you list. Reporting an improvement that was added or removed is due by December 31, and fixing the record first means the buyer's title search and the tax bill agree.

sections.h2: Common situations for Lauderdale County sellers
sections.html:
• Rural acreage with a house in poor shape and an unclear boundary.
  • Inherited family land with several heirs.
  • Manufactured homes with title or assessment gaps.
  • Delinquent tax moving toward the May sale.
  • Owners who moved to Huntsville, Birmingham or Tennessee and want to sell without managing repairs from a distance.

With inherited land, settle who holds title first, since every heir may need to sign. With acreage, a survey or a clear walk of the boundary helps a buyer feel safe.

Cash Home Buyers makes written offers on Lauderdale County houses as they stand, and a local title company clears unpaid tax from the proceeds at closing. A cash sale skips the lender appraisal and the repair requests that often follow it.

sections.h2: What to bring when you call the office
sections.html:
Have the parcel number, your name as it appears on the deed and your last tax receipt in front of you. Ask three things: what is owed now, whether any exemption is on file, and whether any improvements need reporting. If you are the executor of an estate, ask what paperwork the office wants before it will talk to you about the account.

Write down the answers with the date. The closing agent will need the same figures, and a written trail avoids arguments later about what was quoted.

faqs.q: When is Lauderdale County property tax due?
faqs.a: Tax is due October 1 and delinquent after December 31. Unpaid parcels are advertised in April and sold in May.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Lauderdale County?
faqs.a: The Lauderdale County Revenue Commissioner assesses property and collects the tax. You can pay in person, by mail or at alproptax.com.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to pay Lauderdale County tax by credit card?
faqs.a: Yes. A credit card payment, in person or online, adds a 2.50 percent service fee.

faqs.q: What is the regular homestead exemption in Lauderdale County?
faqs.a: The H1 exemption is $4,000 of assessed value for state tax and $3,000 for county tax. It applies to a single-family home you own and occupy on the first day of the tax year, and you should apply before December 31.

faqs.q: What do I need to do after buying property in Lauderdale County?
faqs.a: Record your deed in probate court, assess the property into your name at the Revenue Commissioner's office and claim any exemptions. Finish by December 31 for property bought before October 1.
